metadata.title: Data Leakage: When Your Model Accidentally Sees the Answer
metadata.methodological_boundary: Leakage is distinct from overfitting; high performance alone does not establish leakage; random splitting is not universally wrong; feature availability must match the real prediction setting.
metadata.production_gate: Narrative and beat plan approved; review rendering authorized; clean final master not authorized.

beats.narration_text: Hi, my name is Ushasvi Rachel, and this video is about data leakage and how it can make machine-learning models appear more accurate than they really are. What if your model gets ninety-nine percent accuracy because it accidentally saw the answer? An extraordinary validation score may look like success. But before celebrating, we need to ask what information reached the model.

shot.visual_intent: Bold accuracy hook and leakage question.

beats.narration_text: Data leakage occurs when training or feature construction uses information that would not legitimately be available when a real prediction is made. That information might come from the target, the future, or the evaluation set.

shot.visual_intent: Prediction-time information boundary and leakage arrow.

beats.narration_text: Leakage is dangerous because validation can look unrealistically strong while deployment performance collapses. A team may believe it solved the prediction problem when it actually evaluated a pipeline that cannot exist in the real world. The metric may be calculated correctly, but the evaluation setup is wrong.

shot.visual_intent: False-confidence progression from validation to deployment.

beats.narration_text: The first type is target leakage: a feature directly or indirectly reveals the outcome. Imagine predicting whether a customer will cancel a subscription while using account closed date. That field may make cancellation easy to identify, but it would not be known at the moment the prediction is needed. This example is hypothetical.

shot.visual_intent: Hypothetical churn table highlighting target leakage.

beats.narration_text: Future, or temporal, leakage crosses the prediction-time boundary. Suppose we predict tomorrow’s sales using data recorded only after tomorrow occurred. The feature may correlate strongly with sales, but it is information from the future being used to predict an earlier event. This example is also hypothetical.

shot.visual_intent: Timeline with prediction boundary and backward future-data arrow.

beats.narration_text: Train-test contamination happens when held-out information influences preprocessing, feature selection, or model training. The test set is meant to represent unseen data. Once information crosses from that set into decisions made during training, the evaluation is no longer genuinely independent.

A common example is scaling or imputing the full dataset before separating train and test records. The fitted statistics then contain information from the held-out data. The safer sequence is to split first, fit preprocessing only on the training set, and use that fitted transformation on validation or test data without refitting it.

A leakage-resistant workflow follows the deployment logic. Split the data appropriately. Fit preprocessing and feature selection on training data. Transform held-out data without learning from it. Train the model, then evaluate it on records that remained unseen throughout model development.

shot.visual_intent: Correct end-to-end feature and evaluation workflow.

beats.narration_text: For time-dependent prediction, a standard random train-test split may mix earlier and later observations in ways that violate the real task. A chronological split can train on earlier periods and evaluate on later ones. Random splitting is not always wrong; temporal splitting is especially important when prediction depends on time ordering.

A useful feature audit asks one question: would this value genuinely exist at the moment the prediction is made? If it was created later, derived from the outcome, or updated after the prediction point, it should not enter the model as though it were known in advance.

Leakage is not the same as overfitting. Overfitting means a model learns the available training data too specifically and fails to generalize. Leakage means the model received information it should never have had. Both can produce disappointing real-world performance, but they arise from different failures and require different diagnoses.

shot.visual_intent: Side-by-side distinction between leakage and overfitting.

beats.narration_text: Warning signs include suspiciously strong validation, a dramatic drop after deployment, features closely tied to the outcome, preprocessing performed before splitting, or future information appearing in historical features. These are reasons to investigate, not proof by themselves. A high-performing model does not automatically contain leakage.

shot.visual_intent: Leakage warning-sign cards with caution boundary.

beats.narration_text: Reliable evaluation begins with an honest information boundary. Before asking how accurate your model is, ask whether it had access to information it would actually have in the real world. I’m Ushasvi Rachel with Humanitarians dot A I.

shot.visual_intent: Final real-world information boundary and branded takeaway.
